title: Writing meta descriptions people will click
excerpt: The sentence under a search title should name the outcome and who it is for. Do not repeat the title, and do not stuff keywords.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a clear first line before the day fills in.
caption: Sunrise on a quiet beach, the kind of clear opening a search snippet needs. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a meta description say?
faqs.answer: Say the outcome of the page and who it is for, in one or two sentences. Do not repeat the title, and do not turn the line into a list of keywords. If you cannot name the outcome, the page is not ready to describe.

faqs.question: Will Google always use the description I write?
faqs.answer: No. Google may write its own snippet, and it may shorten whatever it shows to fit the device. Write the sentence anyway, with the outcome in the first clause, so the part that survives is the part that matters. A stuffed or boilerplate line is easier for a system, and a person, to discard.

faqs.question: Where should the description live on a Next.js site?
faqs.answer: Put a unique description in the metadata for each route, beside that page's title. A single description set on the root layout will repeat under every result. If two pages need the same sentence, ask whether you really need two URLs.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A meta description is the sentence under the title in a search result. It should name the outcome and who the page is for. These meta description examples follow that shape: one result, one reader, and no second copy of the title.

Google may still write its own snippet. Write the sentence anyway. It is the line you want a stranger to read before they decide the page is theirs.

## The sentence under the title

Search results give a person a title and, often, a short paragraph beneath it. The title is the claim. The description is the reason to click, in ordinary language. If the title already says what the page is, the next line has to say what the reader leaves with, and who that reader is.

That is a different job from the headline on the page. The headline can carry the studio's voice. The description is closer to a caption: outcome, audience, and the limit of the promise. A studio site has few pages. Each one can afford a sentence that only that page could wear.

Write it as one or two sentences. A comma-separated list of services is a brochure, and brochures get skipped. A question the page does not answer is a tease. Say the thing the page actually does.

Read the pair out loud. Title, pause, description. If the second line could be deleted and nothing would be lost, it is repeating the title. Replace it.

## Outcome first, then the person

Start with the result. "You leave with a homepage that explains the product on one screen." Then name who it is for. "Written for a founder who has outgrown a template." Outcome first, because that is what the eye catches in a stack of links. The person second, so the wrong reader can walk away without a click.

A redesign page might say: "How to change a site without losing the people who already trust it, for a team with a live product and a small audience." A product page might say: "What belongs on the first screen of a tool someone opens between two phone calls." Both sentences can sit under a shorter title. Neither one restates that title.

If you cannot name the outcome, the page is not ready to be described. Fix the page. A clever line cannot rescue a vague one. Founders feel this immediately, because they have clicked too many results that promised a method and delivered a definition of the method.

Keep the claim checkable. "A checklist you can run the week before launch" is checkable. "Unlock your digital potential" is not. The first tells the reader what they will hold. The second could sit under any agency in any city, which is how a snippet teaches people to ignore you.

## Do not repeat the title, and do not stuff

Repetition feels like a mistake because it is one. The reader has already seen the title. Spending the next line on the same words wastes the only other chance you have. It also trains the habit of putting the same phrase in both fields, which makes the result look assembled.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and concise. It warns against keyword stuffing, and against boilerplate that repeats across pages so a person cannot tell two results apart. The same discipline belongs one line lower. A few accurate words help a stranger. The same phrase three times does not. Google also notes that a title link is truncated to fit the device, and that Google may replace a title that is vague, obsolete, inaccurate, or stuffed. Treat the description with the same expectation. Write it for a person. Accept that it may be shortened, and sometimes replaced.

Stuffing has a look. The sentence names every synonym of the service, then the city, then the stack. Nobody speaks that way, so nobody trusts it. If the page is about a Next.js marketing site, the article can say so in the body, where there is room to explain what the founder actually gets: a fast public site, a repository they own, and words they can edit. The snippet does not need the inventory.

Check the language as well. Google's title guidance says the title should match the language and writing system of the page. A description in a different language than the article is the same kind of mismatch. Write the sentence in the language the page is actually in.

## Sentences you can copy the shape of

These are patterns, not lines to paste onto a site that does something else.

A studio homepage: "Design and engineering for founders who need a site that explains the product and a path to a conversation. See the work, then book a call."

A project page: "An ecommerce redesign for a small retailer, including the move and the pages that had to stay trustworthy. What was kept, and what was rebuilt."

A how-to: "A short way to brief a studio so the launch date survives. What to bring, what to leave undecided, and what done means."

An author page: "Who writes here, and which pieces they stand behind. A byline you can follow to a real practice, not a shared login called Admin."

A services page: "What a fixed site project includes, and what an ongoing partnership is for. Written for a founder choosing between the two."

Notice what is missing. No city swapped in to manufacture a second page. No "best," "ultimate," or "complete guide" unless the page is actually complete. No pile of tool names. Hanabi's public projects are easier to describe by the decision than by a keyword list. Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site. Ballarat Box Sports is a community sports brand. A sentence that names the decision will always beat a sentence that names the category five times.

Use the same test on your own pages. Could this sentence sit on a competitor's site unchanged? If yes, it is not done. Add the constraint that makes it yours: the audience, the artifact, or the limit.

## Length, and the part that gets cut

Aim for a sentence a person can finish. On a phone, the snippet is short. Put the outcome in the first clause, not after a warm-up. If you write a second sentence, it should add the audience or the limit, not a new topic.

Do not write to a character superstition at the expense of the sentence. A clean line that gets cut still starts well. A padded line written to hit a count starts badly, and the bad part is what shows. Read the first hundred and forty characters alone. If they are a complete thought, you are in good shape. If they end on "and" or "for teams who," move the point forward.

Skip quotation marks that fight the markup, and skip a line that is only a list of keywords. Emoji and decorative punctuation do not make a studio look more serious. They make the result look like an ad standing in a row of articles.

There is a useful contrast with the title. Google says there is no fixed limit on how long a title element may be, and that the visible title link is cut to the device. The same is true of the snippet you hope to influence. Front-load the meaning. Let the end be the part that can disappear.

## Where the sentence lives in the site

On a Next.js site, the description belongs in that page's metadata, beside the title, and it should be unique per route. A layout that sets one description for the whole site will put the homepage sentence under every article. That is boilerplate, moved from the title into the snippet. A founder looking at their own brand search will see five results that all say the same thing. They will not know which to open. Neither will anyone else.

Write the description when you write the page, not in a cleanup pass the night before launch. The person who knows the outcome is the person drafting. If a CMS holds the field, put it on the editorial checklist next to title, slug, and the one link you mean to offer. On a Hanabi project the marketing site is built so a small team can edit the words that change, without a page-builder pile. This field should be a normal part of publishing, not a hidden tag only a developer can find.

Do not reuse a description because it "tested well" on another URL. The sentence has to be true of this address. If two pages need the same description, you may not need two pages. That question leads straight into the next piece, about keeping one official URL.

Keep a simple record. Three columns are enough: URL, title, description. When someone changes the page, they change the row. A description that still describes last year's offer is the same class of problem as an obsolete title. Google's title guidance calls out titles that were never updated for a new year while the visible heading moved on. The snippet rots the same way, only quieter, because fewer people look at it until the clicks drop.

## A review before you publish

Read every description beside its title and its URL. Mark any row that repeats the title, names no outcome, or could belong to any studio. Rewrite those. Leave the ones that only this page could wear.

Then read them as a set. A studio site should sound like one voice. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. If the homepage is quiet and the blog shouts, the descriptions will show it before the pages do. [Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the heading is a helpful summary, and whether you would share the page with a friend. The snippet is that summary, one step earlier. It also asks you not to write for a mythical preferred length, and not to churn pages so the site looks fresh. A description that exaggerates, or that promises an answer the page does not contain, fails that test in the search result itself.

Use this pass before you ship:

1. The first clause states the outcome.
2. The reader can tell who it is for.
3. The title is not repeated.
4. The sentence is true of this URL only.
5. You would be willing to have it quoted back to you on a sales call.

When the set is honest, the site still has to match it. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover the design and the build of that kind of site, from the first page through the fields a small team can keep editing after launch.

Once the sentence is right, only one URL should be allowed to wear it. [Canonical URLs for a studio site](/blog/canonical-urls-for-a-studio-site) is the next piece, because a good description attached to three versions of the same page splits the click you just earned.
